title: Practical Coding — Full Stack Web Developer (2026)
description: 24 weeks, three 90-minute lessons a week: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node/Express/MongoDB and a full-stack capstone. Built on the freeCodeCamp Full Stack Developer curriculum, with Git, early deployment, mobile-first CSS and a real back end added, and a check on every lesson.

lessons.title: How the web works, and your tools
lessons.summary: What happens between typing an address and seeing a page, and the three tools you will use every session: a browser, a code editor and the browser's developer tools.
objectives: You will explain what a browser, a server and a URL are
You will open the developer tools and inspect a page
You will create, save and open your first .html file
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Install a code editor (VS Code, or an online editor if you are on a phone)
- Open any website, right-click, choose **Inspect**, and change some text in the Elements panel
- Create `index.html`, type a sentence into it, save it and open it in your browser

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: When you visit a website, which program requests the page and draws it on your screen?
Changing text in the developer tools' Elements panel…
options: Changes only your copy until you reload
Saves the change to the server
checks.answer: Changes only your copy until you reload

lessons.title: Basic HTML 1: tags, headings, paragraphs and links
lessons.summary: HTML describes what each part of a page is. Start with the elements every page uses.
objectives: You will write opening and closing tags
You will use h1–h6 and p correctly
You will link to another page with an a element
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **30 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Work through the first Basic HTML workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Build a page about yourself with one h1, two h2 sections and a link to a site you like

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: Which element is the main heading of a page?
Which attribute gives a link its destination?
Write the HTML for a link with the text 'NGG' that goes to https://example.org
checks.rubric: An a element; href is the URL in quotes; the visible text is NGG; the tag is closed.

lessons.title: Basic HTML 2: lists, images and nesting
lessons.summary: Group items into lists, put pictures on the page, and nest elements inside each other properly.
objectives: You will build ordered and unordered lists
You will add an image with alt text
You will nest elements without overlapping tags
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **30 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Continue the Basic HTML workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Add a list of three things you want to build, and a picture with a sensible alt text, to your page

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: Which list shows numbers beside each item?
Why does every img need alt text?
options: It makes the image load faster
Screen readers read it, and it shows if the image fails to load
It is only needed for logos
checks.answer: Screen readers read it, and it shows if the image fails to load

lessons.title: Finishing basic HTML: the structure of a page
lessons.summary: Every page has the same skeleton. Learn what goes in the head and what goes in the body, and why.
objectives: You will write a complete HTML document from memory
You will explain what belongs in head and in body
You will set the page title and character set
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **24 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Finish the Basic HTML workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Rewrite your page with `<!DOCTYPE html>`, `<html lang="en">`, a head with charset and title, and a body

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: Where does the <title> element go?
Write the smallest complete HTML document with the title 'My page'
checks.rubric: Has a doctype, html with lang, head containing meta charset and title 'My page', and an empty body; tags are properly closed.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
lessons.summary: Use elements that say what content is — header, nav, main, section, article, footer — so people, search engines and screen readers understand your page.
objectives: You will choose between section, article and div
You will lay out a page with header, nav, main and footer
You will explain why semantic HTML helps accessibility
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **39 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Semantic HTML workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Restructure your page so it has header, nav, main and footer

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: Which element should hold the main content of a page, once per page?
A blog post that would make sense on its own belongs in…

lessons.title: Git and GitHub: saving your work properly
lessons.summary: Developers keep every version of their code with Git and share it on GitHub. Set it up now, so everything you build from here has a history.
objectives: You will create a GitHub account and a repository
You will commit and push your page
You will read a commit history
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Create a GitHub account (with a parent's permission if you are under 13 — GitHub's minimum age is 13)
- Make a repository called `my-first-site` and upload your index.html
- Change one line, commit it with a clear message, and look at the history

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: What is a commit?
options: A saved snapshot of your files with a message
checks.answer: A saved snapshot of your files with a message

checks.prompt: Write a good commit message for adding a contact form to your page, and say why it is good.
checks.answer: Add contact form to the home page — it says what changed, in the present tense, briefly.
checks.rubric: A short, specific message describing the change; the reason mentions that it explains what changed so it can be found later.

lessons.title: Forms 1: inputs, labels and choices
lessons.summary: Forms are how a page collects information. Build one that works for everybody, including people using screen readers.
objectives: You will build text, email and number inputs
You will connect every input to a label
You will use select, radio buttons, checkboxes and textarea
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **30 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the first Forms and Tables workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Build a sign-up form for a club, with a label for every field

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: How do you connect a <label> to its input?
options: Put them next to each other
Give the label a for attribute matching the input's id
Use the same class on both
checks.answer: Give the label a for attribute matching the input's id

checks.prompt: Which input lets someone choose only ONE option from a group?

lessons.title: Forms 2 and tables
lessons.summary: Finish forms, then lay out data in tables — the right tool for timetables and results, and the wrong tool for page layout.
objectives: You will group fields with fieldset and legend
You will build a table with a header row
You will explain when a table is the right choice
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **29 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

- Finish the Forms and Tables workshops on freeCodeCamp
- Add a weekly timetable table to your page, with th scope="col" on the header row

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: Which element is a header cell in a table?
Should you use a table to arrange the columns of a page layout?
options: No — tables are for tabular data; use CSS for layout
checks.answer: No — tables are for tabular data; use CSS for layout

lessons.title: Accessible HTML
lessons.summary: About one in six people lives with a disability. Make pages that work with a keyboard and a screen reader, using the right elements and ARIA only where HTML has no answer.
objectives: You will check a page using only the keyboard
You will use headings in order and give images alt text
You will explain when ARIA is and is not needed
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **28 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the HTML accessibility workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Use Tab to move through your page — can you reach and use everything?

## Before the next lesson

Answer the check below. If you get stuck, write down exactly where — that is the question to bring to your instructor.

checks.prompt: What is the first rule of ARIA?
options: If a native HTML element does the job, use it instead of ARIA
checks.answer: If a native HTML element does the job, use it instead of ARIA

checks.prompt: Someone who cannot use a mouse moves through links and buttons with…

lessons.title: Project: your first page, live on the internet
lessons.summary: Put your HTML page online with GitHub Pages, so you have a real address to share by week four.
objectives: You will publish a site with GitHub Pages

lessons.body:

checks.prompt: Paste the link to your published page. It must have semantic structure (header, main, footer), a list, an image with alt text, a form with labels and a table.
checks.rubric: Live link works; semantic elements used; image has meaningful alt text; every form field has a label; table has header cells; no broken tags.

checks.prompt: Which selector targets every element with class="card"?

lessons.title: Responsive design, mobile first
lessons.summary: Most people here use the web on a phone. Design for the small screen first, then add room with media queries.

This lesson is about **45 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

checks.prompt: Write a media query that makes .grid two columns from 600px wide and up.
checks.rubric: Uses @media with min-width 600px; inside, .grid gets two columns (grid or flex is acceptable); valid syntax.

lessons.title: Flexbox

options: Lets items move onto a new line when there is no room
Makes every item the same width
checks.answer: Lets items move onto a new line when there is no room

lessons.title: Typography

checks.answer: rem respects the reader's own text-size setting

lessons.title: Styling forms

You will make focus clearly visible

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **50 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.
